A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same legal fact prediction research, despite substantial revisions to the benchmark and experiments. The main text, figures, tables and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-4o experiments comparing QA, simulated trials and few-shot variants on 381 loan cases in Table 1.

after.justification: v2 reports original multi-model judgment-prediction experiments, subgroup and bias analyses, and instruction-following evaluations in Tables 2–5 and 8 and Figures 5–6.

M1.justification: v1 generates fact descriptions and six structured loan fields from evidence. v2 explicitly conditions fact prediction on plaintiff claims and evidence, produces free-form facts, and implements a subsequent judgment-prediction stage yielding per-claim support labels. This operationalizes the downstream pipeline that v1 only motivated.

E1.justification: The reported evaluation replaces LFP-Loan's civil-loan coverage with LFPBench's ten civil causes of action, including contract, inheritance, marital-property and tort disputes. v2 also evaluates claim-level judgment prediction and includes cases without defendant evidence, which v1 explicitly excluded.

E2.justification: v1 compares GPT-4o QA and simulation methods, each with and without few-shot examples. v2 drops those simulation/few-shot comparisons and compares three LJP pipelines using GPT-4o, Claude3.5, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama3.1-Chinese-8B, Law-Llama3.1-8B and LawJustice-Llama3.1-8B. Appendix B.2 additionally compares instruction following for DISC-LawLLM, Lawyer-Llama-13B-V2 and AIE-51-8-Law-Model.

E3.justification: v1 evaluates embedding similarity and strict accuracy on six loan fields. v2 centers evaluation on three-class judgment accuracy, adds ChatLaw embeddings alongside the retained OpenAI embedding model, and introduces evidence-order permutations and screening by parseable-output rate. Table 7 specifies separate decoding settings for the newly evaluated open models; the corresponding closed-model settings retain v1's values.

E4.justification: v1's few-shot comparison is removed. v2 adds analyses by judgment outcome, case type and defendant evidence, correlations between fact similarity and judgment accuracy, evidence-order and evidence-quantity bias studies, and instruction-following diagnostics. Tables 3–5 and 8 and Figures 5–6 substantially expand the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, variability estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's averages across models and descriptive correlation plots do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1's loan-fact results, including QA plus few-shot's 0.7214 average key-item accuracy, are removed. v2 Table 2 newly reports general-model average judgment accuracies of 46.72%, 48.16% and 50.46% for evidence-based, LFP-empowered and fact-based LJP, respectively. Subgroup, bias and instruction-following results are also added. These use different tasks and settings and do not establish performance gains over v1.

T1.justification: v2 Section 2.2 revises the formal task domain to f(C, Z), explicitly including plaintiff claims, and defines downstream judgments g(C, f(C, Z)) with an objective of maximizing judgment accuracy. v1 defines evidence-to-fact prediction without this downstream objective. The formal addition is limited to task formulation; neither version contains theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on introducing LFP, constructing a loan benchmark and demonstrating task difficulty. v2 makes evaluated LFP-empowered judgment prediction a central contribution, adds a 38.5% performance-gap reduction claim and highlights evidence-related model biases. The 38.5% figure corresponds to the general-purpose-model averages in Table 2.

C2.justification: Loan-arithmetic, few-shot and simulated-trial explanations give way to hypotheses about legal-model fine-tuning, counterevidence, nontextual evidence and attention-related bias. v2 also acknowledges information lost when evidence is summarized in judgments. Some new interpretation is inconsistent: Finding 5 says performance is better with defendant evidence, while Table 2's general-model averages show the opposite.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's GPT-4o defaults and prediction/simulation prompts, v2 supplies annotation criteria and annotator backgrounds, anonymization procedures, model versions and asset documentation, separate open-model settings, and extraction/LFP/LJP prompt templates. It also adds a code-and-data access link. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation, although the LFP-empowered judgment prompt remains ambiguous.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial Related Work section covering judgment-prediction benchmarks, predictions from briefs and complaints, and legal document summarization. It explicitly distinguishes LFP's reconstruction and conflict resolution from summarization. The bibliography is extensively revised, while the central motivation from Medvedeva and Mcbride is retained.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Task and dataset sections gain subsections, experiments are organized around two research questions and eight findings, and Related Work and Ethical Considerations are added. Appendices are reorganized around dataset and experiment documentation; the trial-stage Discussion largely retains its earlier substance.

P2.justification: v2 redraws and enlarges the pipeline and trial diagrams, removes the simulation diagram, replaces the loan example with a house-lease display, and adds dataset-distribution, correlation and bias figures. Results use new grouped tables, and appendices switch to full-width tables and prompt boxes. These are substantial display and layout changes.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical scope and untested downstream motivation through broader civil-case coverage and direct comparisons of judgment-prediction pipelines. The added diagnostics and appendix documentation improve scientific usefulness and transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of loan-field diagnostics and reporting problems, including Table 4's inconsistent PC average and ambiguous LJP prompts. The downstream benefit is supported for the general-purpose models; the legal-model results and absence of uncertainty estimates limit broader conclusions.
